newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Zaire weekend peace talks in doubt.
newsitem.headline: Zaire weekend peace talks in doubt.

text.p: Weekend talks in South Africa aimed at making peace in Zaire may be delayed by political confusion and continued fighting in the Central African country, diplomats said on Friday.

They raised the possibility of a postponement of the negotiations, tentatively scheduled to begin on Saturday, amid uncertainty that representatives of rebel leader Laurent Kabila had even arrived in South Africa as planned.
The Zaire government team, led by President Mobutu Sese Seko's adviser Honore Ngbanda, was in Pretoria ready and waiting to get started, a Zaire embassy spokesman said.
Asked if Kabila's people were not in place, he told Reuters: "That's the impression we're being given."
"Perhaps we will hear something by tomorrow," he added.
Mobutu's son Nganza again called for a ceasefire in the war.
He said he knew nothing of reports that government troops, fearing an imminent rebel advance, had begun looting the diamond-mining town of Mbuji-Mayi in central Zaire.

"I heard of all this this morning that I have to check, but I have no precise report on that. But I hope that this weekend coming the two parties will find a peaceful solution," he told BBC World television.

A Reuters reporter in Lubumbashi quoted expatriate sources as saying soldiers in Mbuji-Mayi had looted vehicles from the state mining company and fled westward, while rebel units had been spotted in villages outside the city.

South Africa's Foreign Affairs Ministry, which is acting as "facilitator" for the peace talks, declined all comment on the likely start of the negotiations or the presence of representatives from both sides in the Johannesburg area.
But in London a senior South African diplomat said there could indeed be a delay in the peace talks.
"Maybe there will be...a later date that will be set aside for the discussions," Happy Mahlangu, South Africa's deputy high commissioner in London, told the BBC.
"On our (South Africa's) side, what we needed to do was facilitate the discussions and of course there won't be any discussions if the two parties are not there," he said.

Kabila has said that nothing short of the departure from office of Mobutu, ruler of Zaire for the past 31 years, will satisfy his rebel movement, which has met very little resistance in its capture of a quarter of the country.

On the eve of the talks, Kabila flatly rejected a surprise power-sharing offer from Zaire's new Prime Minister Etienne Tshisekedi, a veteran opponent of Mobutu who has called Kabila his brother and dismissed talks in South Africa as unnecessary.
Mobutu's son Nzanga said the government had to get agreement with Kabila's rebels in order to permit elections.
"People in Zaire want elections. And since those elections are impossible as long as we don't have a ceasefire...we have to find an agreement with Kabila's people," he said.
